title: Grace Darling Rows Out into the Storm
text:
Grace Darling was the daughter of William Darling, keeper of the Longstone lighthouse on the Farne Islands off the coast of Northumberland. She grew up on the bare rock, helping her father keep the light.

Early on 7 September 1838, the steamship Forfarshire, bound from Hull to Dundee with engine trouble, was driven onto Big Harcar, a rock near the lighthouse, and broke in two. Many passengers were swept away. At first light Grace, then twenty-two, saw survivors clinging to the rock. The sea was too rough for the lifeboat from the mainland to set out at once.

Grace and her father launched their small rowing boat, a coble, and rowed about a mile along a sheltered route to the rock. William climbed onto it while Grace held the boat steady in the waves. They took off a woman and four men and brought them back to the lighthouse. Then William and two of the rescued crewmen went back for the remaining four. In all, nine people were saved.

The rescue made Grace famous across Britain. Gifts, letters and requests for locks of her hair poured in, and Queen Victoria sent money. Grace found the attention hard to bear. She died of tuberculosis in 1842, at twenty-six, and is buried at Bamburgh.
lesson: Courage is often shared: one person rows, another holds steady. Families that face danger side by side can do what neither could alone.
source: Contemporary newspaper reports; William Darling's lighthouse journal; Jessica Mitford, Grace Had an English Heart (1988)
caveat: Accounts differ on how much of the rowing Grace did, and the fame that followed added romantic details.
